newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka refugees eye new life at northern border.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka refugees eye new life at northern border.

text.p: Buses carrying Tamil civilians start arriving well before noon at this remote northern Sri Lankan village bording the war-ravaged Wanni region, stronghold of the separatist Tamil Tiger rebels.
Every day the buses bring some 800 men, women and children to the Thandikulam checkpoint, about 225 km (140 miles) northeast of the capital Colombo.

"Many of them are here on business. They go into town, buy provisions and return in the evening or the next day. But a large number of them never go back. They want to begin a new life elsewhere in Sri Lanka," said a senior army officer in charge of the checkpoint's routine clearance work.
He estimated that at least half of them never return home.

For the people of the Wanni region, the border village is the gateway to the rest of this Indian Ocean island. They have access to shops brimming with basics like candles, soap and textiles -- goods that are scarce on the other side.
But for many others, it is the way out of the harsh and impoverished Wanni and the beginning of a sometimes long search for a new life.
Middle-aged Andi Kandalingam joined the queue of would-be refugees with his wife and five little children.
"Life up there is a very difficult one. It is not a fit place to bring up children," he said.
The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) are fighting for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in predominantly Sinhalese Sri Lanka's north and east.
The LTTE rebels control vast areas of the Wanni.

Aid workers say the Wanni's population has swelled by an estimated 400,000 refugees since March 1996, when government troops completed the capture of the northern Jaffna peninsula, the rebels' former stronghold.
About 17,000 more people fled to rebel-controlled areas in the Wanni in February this year after the military captured a key highway linking two northern towns, aid workers say.
The rebels have often accused Colombo of neglecting the Wanni's civilians, claiming they faced starvation.
The government says it is forced to limit supplies to the region, fearing most of it will fall into rebel hands.
As families like Kandalingam's pour through the gates of Thandikulam, "transit" camps further south in Vavuniya town, designed to house refugees for a limited time period, are becoming overcrowded.

"There are more than 14,000 refugees housed in ten camps in Vavuniya," said inspector L.A. Guneratne of the Vavuniya police. "We're trying our best to clear them and send them out of here, but new people keep arriving."

More than 57,000 Tamil refugees have crossed the Thandikulam checkpoint since October last year, when the border was opened to civilian traffic, military spokesman Brigadier Tissa Jayatunga told Reuters.
"Of that number, we have so far cleared 42,616 people to go whereever they wish," he said.

Widow Thyagaraja Muthupillai and her 20-year-old son arrived a month ago at the Veppankulam transit camp in Vavuniya, where some 3,000 refugees are housed. She is waiting to be "sponsored" by her sister, who lives in Vavuniya.
"When my sister agrees to take me, they will release us from here. Then my son can start a whole new life here. I only hope it will be better for him here than in the Wanni," she said.
But middle-aged Arumugam Vadivel and his seven children have been at Veppankulam camp for nearly three months.
"They won't release me to go live somewhere else in the country, because I have no relatives to take responsibility of me and my family. But I don't want to go back to the Wanni either," he said.
The government says more than 50,000 people have died in the war, now in its 14th year. The LTTE says the number is much higher, with a majority of the dead being Tamils.
